Policy Gradients and Actor-Critic

The previous chapters optimized policies through Q-functions, soft Bellman relations, or path-consistency equations. Can expected return itself supply the policy objective without differentiating the environment dynamics? The score function estimator applies directly to trajectories because the policy terms are the only factors in their probability law that depend on the policy parameters.

The estimator requires only the ability to evaluate and differentiate log⁡πw(a∣s)\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a|s)logπw​(a∣s), so it also works with discrete actions where reparameterization is unavailable.

Let G(τ)≡∑t=0Tr(st,at)G(\tau) \equiv \sum_{t=0}^T r(s_t, a_t)G(τ)≡∑t=0T​r(st​,at​) be the sum of undiscounted rewards in a trajectory τ\tauτ. The stochastic optimization problem we face is to maximize:

J(w)=Eτ∼p(τ;w)[G(τ)]J(\boldsymbol{w}) = \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim p(\tau;\boldsymbol{w})}[G(\tau)]J(w)=Eτ∼p(τ;w)​[G(τ)]
(1)

where τ=(s0,a0,s1,a1,...)\tau = (s_0,a_0,s_1,a_1,...)τ=(s0​,a0​,s1​,a1​,...) is a trajectory and G(τ)G(\tau)G(τ) is the total return. Applying the score function estimator, we get:

∇wJ(w)=∇wEτ[G(τ)]=Eτ[G(τ)∇wlog⁡p(τ;w)]=Eτ[G(τ)∇w∑t=0Tlog⁡πw(at∣st)]=Eτ[G(τ)∑t=0T∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st)]\begin{align*} \nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}J(\boldsymbol{w}) &= \nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\mathbb{E}_{\tau}[G(\tau)] \\ &= \mathbb{E}_{\tau}\left[G(\tau)\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log p(\tau;\boldsymbol{w})\right] \\ &= \mathbb{E}_{\tau}\left[G(\tau)\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\sum_{t=0}^T\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)\right] \\ &= \mathbb{E}_{\tau}\left[G(\tau)\sum_{t=0}^T\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)\right] \end{align*}∇w​J(w)​=∇w​Eτ​[G(τ)]=Eτ​[G(τ)∇w​logp(τ;w)]=Eτ​[G(τ)∇w​t=0∑T​logπw​(at​∣st​)]=Eτ​[G(τ)t=0∑T​∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​)]​
(2)

We have eliminated the need to know the transition probabilities in this estimator since the probability of a trajectory factorizes as:

p(τ;w)=p(s0)∏t=0Tπw(at∣st)p(st+1∣st,at)p(\tau;\boldsymbol{w}) = p(s_0)\prod_{t=0}^T \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t)p(τ;w)=p(s0​)t=0∏T​πw​(at​∣st​)p(st+1​∣st​,at​)
(3)

Therefore, only the policy depends on w\boldsymbol{w}w. When taking the logarithm of this product, we get a sum where all the w\boldsymbol{w}w-independent terms vanish. The final estimator samples trajectories under the distribution p(τ;w)p(\tau; \boldsymbol{w})p(τ;w) and computes:

∇wJ(w)≈1N∑i=1N[G(τ(i))∑t=0T∇wlog⁡πw(at(i)∣st(i))]\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}J(\boldsymbol{w}) \approx \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N\left[G(\tau^{(i)})\sum_{t=0}^T\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t^{(i)}|s_t^{(i)})\right]∇w​J(w)≈N1​i=1∑N​[G(τ(i))t=0∑T​∇w​logπw​(at(i)​∣st(i)​)]
(4)

This is a direct application of the score function estimator. However, we rarely use this form in practice and instead make several improvements to further reduce the variance.

Leveraging Conditional Independence¶

Given the Markov property of the MDP, rewards rkr_krk​ for k<tk < tk<t are conditionally independent of action ata_tat​ given the history ht=(s0,a0,...,st−1,at−1,st)h_t = (s_0,a_0,...,s_{t-1},a_{t-1},s_t)ht​=(s0​,a0​,...,st−1​,at−1​,st​). This allows us to only need to consider future rewards when computing policy gradients.

∇wJ(w)=Eτ[∑t=0T∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st)∑k=0Trk]=Eτ[∑t=0T∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st)(∑k=0t−1rk+∑k=tTrk)]=Eτ[∑t=0T∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st)∑k=tTrk]\begin{align*} \nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}J(\boldsymbol{w}) &= \mathbb{E}_{\tau}\left[\sum_{t=0}^T\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)\sum_{k=0}^T r_k\right] \\ &= \mathbb{E}_{\tau}\left[\sum_{t=0}^T\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)\left(\sum_{k=0}^{t-1} r_k + \sum_{k=t}^T r_k\right)\right] \\ &= \mathbb{E}_{\tau}\left[\sum_{t=0}^T\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)\sum_{k=t}^T r_k\right] \end{align*}∇w​J(w)​=Eτ​[t=0∑T​∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​)k=0∑T​rk​]=Eτ​[t=0∑T​∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​)(k=0∑t−1​rk​+k=t∑T​rk​)]=Eτ​[t=0∑T​∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​)k=t∑T​rk​]​
(5)

The conditional independence assumption means that the term Eτ[∑t=0T∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st)∑k=0t−1rk]\mathbb{E}_{\tau}\left[\sum_{t=0}^T\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)\sum_{k=0}^{t-1} r_k \right]Eτ​[∑t=0T​∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​)∑k=0t−1​rk​] vanishes. To see this, factor the trajectory distribution as:

p(τ)=p(s0,...,st,a0,...,at−1)πw(at∣st)p(st+1,...,sT,at+1,...,aT∣st,at)p(\tau) = p(s_0,...,s_t,a_0,...,a_{t-1}) \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t) p(s_{t+1},...,s_T,a_{t+1},...,a_T|s_t,a_t)p(τ)=p(s0​,...,st​,a0​,...,at−1​)πw​(at​∣st​)p(st+1​,...,sT​,at+1​,...,aT​∣st​,at​)
(6)

We can now re-write a single term of this summation as:

Eτ[∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st)∑k=0t−1rk]=Es0:t,a0:t−1[∑k=0t−1rk Eat[∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st)]]\mathbb{E}_{\tau}\left[\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)\sum_{k=0}^{t-1} r_k\right] = \mathbb{E}_{s_{0:t},a_{0:t-1}}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{t-1} r_k \, \mathbb{E}_{a_t}\left[\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)\right]\right]Eτ​[∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​)k=0∑t−1​rk​]=Es0:t​,a0:t−1​​[k=0∑t−1​rk​Eat​​[∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​)]]
(7)

The inner expectation is zero because

Eat[∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st)]=∫∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st)πw(at∣st)dat=∫∇wπw(at∣st)πw(at∣st)πw(at∣st)dat=∫∇wπw(at∣st)dat=∇w∫πw(at∣st)dat=∇w1=0\begin{align*} \mathbb{E}_{a_t}\left[\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)\right] &= \int \nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)da_t \\ &= \int \frac{\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)}{\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)}\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)da_t \\ &= \int \nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)da_t \\ &= \nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\int \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)da_t \\ &= \nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}1 = 0 \end{align*}Eat​​[∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​)]​=∫∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​)πw​(at​∣st​)dat​=∫πw​(at​∣st​)∇w​πw​(at​∣st​)​πw​(at​∣st​)dat​=∫∇w​πw​(at​∣st​)dat​=∇w​∫πw​(at​∣st​)dat​=∇w​1=0​
(8)

The Monte Carlo estimator becomes:

∇wJ(w)≈1N∑i=1N[∑t=0T∇wlog⁡πw(at(i)∣st(i))∑k=tTrk(i)]\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}J(\boldsymbol{w}) \approx \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N\left[\sum_{t=0}^T\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t^{(i)}|s_t^{(i)})\sum_{k=t}^T r_k^{(i)}\right]∇w​J(w)≈N1​i=1∑N​[t=0∑T​∇w​logπw​(at(i)​∣st(i)​)k=t∑T​rk(i)​]
(9)

This gives us the REINFORCE algorithm:

Algorithm 1 (REINFORCE)

Input: Policy parameterization πw(a∣s)\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a|s)πw​(a∣s)
Output: Updated policy parameters w\boldsymbol{w}w
Hyperparameters: Learning rate α\alphaα, number of episodes NNN, episode length TTT

  1. Initialize parameters w\boldsymbol{w}w

  2. For episode = 1, ..., NNN do:

    1. Collect trajectory τ=(s0,a0,r0,...,sT,aT,rT)\tau = (s_0, a_0, r_0, ..., s_T, a_T, r_T)τ=(s0​,a0​,r0​,...,sT​,aT​,rT​) using policy πw(a∣s)\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a|s)πw​(a∣s)

    2. Compute returns: Gt=∑k=tTrkG_t = \sum_{k=t}^T r_kGt​=∑k=tT​rk​ for t=0,...,Tt = 0, ..., Tt=0,...,T

    3. Compute gradient estimate: g^=∑t=0T∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st)Gt\hat{g} = \sum_{t=0}^T \nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t) G_tg^​=∑t=0T​∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​)Gt​

    4. Update policy: w←w+αg^\boldsymbol{w} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{w} + \alpha \hat{g}w←w+αg^​

  3. Return w\boldsymbol{w}w

The benefit of this estimator compared to the naive one (which would weight each score function by the full trajectory return G(τ)G(\tau)G(τ)) is that it generally has less variance. This variance reduction arises from the conditional independence structure we exploited: past rewards do not depend on future actions. More formally, this estimator is an instance of a variance reduction technique known as the Extended Conditional Monte Carlo Method.

The Surrogate Loss Perspective¶

The algorithm above computes a gradient estimate g^\hat{g}g^​ explicitly. In practice, implementations using automatic differentiation frameworks take a different approach: they define a surrogate loss whose gradient matches the REINFORCE estimator. For a single trajectory, consider:

Lsurrogate(w)=−∑t=0Tlog⁡πw(at∣st) GtL_{\text{surrogate}}(\boldsymbol{w}) = -\sum_{t=0}^T \log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t) \, G_tLsurrogate​(w)=−t=0∑T​logπw​(at​∣st​)Gt​
(10)

where the returns GtG_tGt​ and actions ata_tat​ are treated as fixed constants (detached from the computation graph). Taking the gradient with respect to w\boldsymbol{w}w:

∇wLsurrogate=−∑t=0T∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st) Gt\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}} L_{\text{surrogate}} = -\sum_{t=0}^T \nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t) \, G_t∇w​Lsurrogate​=−t=0∑T​∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​)Gt​
(11)

Minimizing this surrogate loss via gradient descent yields the same update as maximizing expected return via REINFORCE. The negative sign converts our maximization problem into a minimization suitable for standard optimizers.

This surrogate loss is not the expected return J(w)J(\boldsymbol{w})J(w) we are trying to maximize. It is a computational device that produces the correct gradient at the current parameter values. Several properties distinguish it from a true loss function:

  1. It changes each iteration. The returns GtG_tGt​ come from trajectories sampled under the current policy. After updating w\boldsymbol{w}w, we must collect new trajectories and construct a new surrogate loss.

  2. Its value is not meaningful. Unlike supervised learning where the loss measures prediction error, the numerical value of LsurrogateL_{\text{surrogate}}Lsurrogate​ has no direct interpretation. Only its gradient matters.

  3. It is valid only locally. The surrogate loss provides the correct gradient only at the parameters used to collect the data. Moving far from those parameters invalidates the gradient estimate.

This perspective explains why policy gradient code often looks different from the pseudocode above. Instead of computing g^\hat{g}g^​ explicitly, implementations define the surrogate loss and call loss.backward():

# Surrogate loss implementation (single trajectory)
log_probs = [policy.log_prob(a_t, s_t) for s_t, a_t in trajectory]
returns = compute_returns(rewards)
surrogate_loss = -sum(lp * G for lp, G in zip(log_probs, returns))
surrogate_loss.backward()  # computes REINFORCE gradient
optimizer.step()

Variance Reduction via Control Variates¶

Recall that the REINFORCE gradient estimator, after leveraging conditional independence, takes the form:

∇wJ(w)≈1N∑i=1N[∑t=0T∇wlog⁡πw(at(i)∣st(i))∑k=tTrk(i)]\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}J(\boldsymbol{w}) \approx \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N\left[\sum_{t=0}^T\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t^{(i)}|s_t^{(i)})\sum_{k=t}^T r_k^{(i)}\right]∇w​J(w)≈N1​i=1∑N​[t=0∑T​∇w​logπw​(at(i)​∣st(i)​)k=t∑T​rk(i)​]
(12)

This is a sum over trajectories and timesteps. The gradient contribution at timestep ttt of trajectory iii is:

∇wlog⁡πw(at(i)∣st(i))∑k=tTrk(i)\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t^{(i)}|s_t^{(i)})\sum_{k=t}^T r_k^{(i)}∇w​logπw​(at(i)​∣st(i)​)k=t∑T​rk(i)​
(13)

While unbiased, this estimator suffers from high variance because the return ∑k=tTrk\sum_{k=t}^T r_k∑k=tT​rk​ can vary significantly across trajectories even for the same state-action pair. The control variate method provides a principled way to reduce this variance.

General Control Variate Theory¶

For a general estimator ZZZ of some quantity μ=E[Z]\mu = \mathbb{E}[Z]μ=E[Z], and a control variate CCC with known expectation E[C]=0\mathbb{E}[C]=0E[C]=0, we can construct:

Zcv=Z−αCZ_{\text{cv}} = Z - \alpha CZcv​=Z−αC
(14)

This remains unbiased since E[Zcv]=E[Z]−αE[C]=E[Z]\mathbb{E}[Z_{\text{cv}}] = \mathbb{E}[Z] - \alpha\mathbb{E}[C] = \mathbb{E}[Z]E[Zcv​]=E[Z]−αE[C]=E[Z]. The variance is:

Var(Zcv)=Var(Z)+α2Var(C)−2αCov(Z,C)\text{Var}(Z_{\text{cv}}) = \text{Var}(Z) + \alpha^2\text{Var}(C) - 2\alpha\text{Cov}(Z,C)Var(Zcv​)=Var(Z)+α2Var(C)−2αCov(Z,C)
(15)

The −2αCov(Z,C)-2\alpha\text{Cov}(Z,C)−2αCov(Z,C) term is what enables variance reduction. If ZZZ and CCC are positively correlated, we can choose α>0\alpha > 0α>0 to make this term negative and large in magnitude, reducing the overall variance. However, the α2Var(C)\alpha^2\text{Var}(C)α2Var(C) term grows quadratically with α\alphaα, so if we make α\alphaα too large, this quadratic term will eventually dominate and the variance will increase rather than decrease. The variance as a function of α\alphaα is a parabola opening upward, with a unique minimum. Setting ddαVar(Zcv)=0\frac{d}{d\alpha}\text{Var}(Z_{\text{cv}}) = 0dαd​Var(Zcv​)=0 gives:

α∗=Cov(Z,C)Var(C)\alpha^* = \frac{\text{Cov}(Z,C)}{\text{Var}(C)}α∗=Var(C)Cov(Z,C)​
(16)

This is the coefficient from ordinary least squares regression: we predict the estimator ZZZ using the control variate CCC as the predictor. Since E[C]=0\mathbb{E}[C] = 0E[C]=0, the linear model is Z≈E[Z]+α∗CZ \approx \mathbb{E}[Z] + \alpha^* CZ≈E[Z]+α∗C, where α∗\alpha^*α∗ is the OLS slope coefficient. The control variate estimator Zcv=Z−α∗CZ_{\text{cv}} = Z - \alpha^* CZcv​=Z−α∗C computes the residual: the part of ZZZ that cannot be explained by CCC.

Substituting α∗\alpha^*α∗ into the variance formula yields:

Var(Zcv)=Var(Z)−[Cov(Z,C)]2Var(C)=(1−R2)Var(Z)\text{Var}(Z_{\text{cv}}) = \text{Var}(Z) - \frac{[\text{Cov}(Z,C)]^2}{\text{Var}(C)} = (1 - R^2) \text{Var}(Z)Var(Zcv​)=Var(Z)−Var(C)[Cov(Z,C)]2​=(1−R2)Var(Z)
(17)

where R2=[Cov(Z,C)]2Var(Z)Var(C)R^2 = \frac{[\text{Cov}(Z,C)]^2}{\text{Var}(Z)\text{Var}(C)}R2=Var(Z)Var(C)[Cov(Z,C)]2​ is the coefficient of determination from regressing ZZZ on CCC. The variance reduction is R2Var(Z)R^2 \text{Var}(Z)R2Var(Z): the better CCC predicts ZZZ, the more variance we eliminate.

Application to REINFORCE¶

In the reinforcement learning setting, our REINFORCE gradient estimator is a sum over timesteps: ∑t=0TZt\sum_{t=0}^T Z_t∑t=0T​Zt​ where each ZtZ_tZt​ represents the gradient contribution at timestep ttt. We apply control variates separately to each term. Since Var(∑tZt)=∑tVar(Zt)+∑t≠sCov(Zt,Zs)\text{Var}(\sum_t Z_t) = \sum_t \text{Var}(Z_t) + \sum_{t \neq s} \text{Cov}(Z_t, Z_s)Var(∑t​Zt​)=∑t​Var(Zt​)+∑t=s​Cov(Zt​,Zs​), reducing the variance of each ZtZ_tZt​ reduces the total variance, though we do not explicitly address the cross-timestep covariance terms.

For a given trajectory at state sts_tst​, the gradient contribution at time ttt is:

Zt=∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st)∑k=tTrkZ_t = \nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)\sum_{k=t}^T r_kZt​=∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​)k=t∑T​rk​
(18)

This is the product of the score function ∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st)\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​) and the return-to-go ∑k=tTrk\sum_{k=t}^T r_k∑k=tT​rk​. We can subtract any state-dependent function b(st)b(s_t)b(st​) from the return without introducing bias, as long as b(st)b(s_t)b(st​) does not depend on ata_tat​. This is because:

Eat∼πw(⋅∣st)[∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st)b(st)]=b(st)Eat[∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st)]=0\mathbb{E}_{a_t \sim \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(\cdot|s_t)}\left[\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)b(s_t)\right] = b(s_t)\mathbb{E}_{a_t}\left[\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)\right] = 0Eat​∼πw​(⋅∣st​)​[∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​)b(st​)]=b(st​)Eat​​[∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​)]=0
(19)

where the last equality follows from the score function identity (8).

We can now define our control variate as:

Ct=∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st)⋅b(st)C_t = \nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t) \cdot b(s_t)Ct​=∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​)⋅b(st​)
(20)

where b(st)b(s_t)b(st​) is a baseline function that depends only on the state. This satisfies E[Ct∣st]=0\mathbb{E}[C_t|s_t] = 0E[Ct​∣st​]=0. Our control variate estimator becomes:

Zt,cv=Zt−Ct=∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st)(∑k=tTrk−b(st))Z_{t,\text{cv}} = Z_t - C_t = \nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)\left(\sum_{k=t}^T r_k - b(s_t)\right)Zt,cv​=Zt​−Ct​=∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​)(k=t∑T​rk​−b(st​))
(21)

The optimal baseline b∗(st)b^*(s_t)b∗(st​) minimizes the variance. To find it, consider the scalar parameter case for simplicity. Write g(at)≡∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st)g(a_t) \equiv \nabla_w \log \pi_w(a_t|s_t)g(at​)≡∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​) and Gt=∑k=tTrkG_t = \sum_{k=t}^T r_kGt​=∑k=tT​rk​. We want to minimize:

b∗(st)=arg⁡min⁡bVarat∼πw(⋅∣st)[g(at)(Gt−b)]b^*(s_t) = \arg\min_{b} \text{Var}_{a_t \sim \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(\cdot|s_t)}\left[g(a_t)(G_t - b)\right]b∗(st​)=argbmin​Varat​∼πw​(⋅∣st​)​[g(at​)(Gt​−b)]
(22)

Since the mean does not depend on bbb, minimizing the variance is equivalent to minimizing the second moment E[g(at)2(Gt−b)2∣st]\mathbb{E}[g(a_t)^2(G_t - b)^2|s_t]E[g(at​)2(Gt​−b)2∣st​]. Expanding and taking the derivative with respect to bbb gives:

b∗(st)=Eat∣st[g(at)2Gt]Eat∣st[g(at)2]b^*(s_t) = \frac{\mathbb{E}_{a_t|s_t}\left[g(a_t)^2 G_t\right]}{\mathbb{E}_{a_t|s_t}\left[g(a_t)^2\right]}b∗(st​)=Eat​∣st​​[g(at​)2]Eat​∣st​​[g(at​)2Gt​]​
(23)

For vector-valued parameters w\boldsymbol{w}w, we minimize a scalar proxy such as the trace of the covariance matrix, which yields the same formula with ∥∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st)∥2\|\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)\|^2∥∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​)∥2 in place of g(at)2g(a_t)^2g(at​)2:

b∗(st)=Eat∣st[∥∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st)∥2Gt]Eat∣st[∥∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st)∥2]b^*(s_t) = \frac{\mathbb{E}_{a_t|s_t}\left[\|\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)\|^2 G_t\right]}{\mathbb{E}_{a_t|s_t}\left[\|\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)\|^2\right]}b∗(st​)=Eat​∣st​​[∥∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​)∥2]Eat​∣st​​[∥∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​)∥2Gt​]​
(24)

This is the exact optimal baseline: a weighted average of returns where the weights are the squared norms of the score function. In practice, we treat the squared norm as roughly constant across actions at a given state, which leads to the simpler and widely used choice:

b(st)≈E[Gt∣st]=vπw(st)b(s_t) \approx \mathbb{E}[G_t|s_t] = v^{\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}}(s_t)b(st​)≈E[Gt​∣st​]=vπw​(st​)
(25)

With this approximation, the variance-reduced gradient contribution at timestep ttt becomes:

Zcv,t=∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st)(∑k=tTrk−vπw(st))Z_{\text{cv},t} = \nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)\left(\sum_{k=t}^T r_k - v^{\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}}(s_t)\right)Zcv,t​=∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​)(k=t∑T​rk​−vπw​(st​))
(26)

The term in parentheses is exactly the advantage function: Aπw(st,at)=qπw(st,at)−vπw(st)A^{\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}}(s_t, a_t) = q^{\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}}(s_t, a_t) - v^{\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}}(s_t)Aπw​(st​,at​)=qπw​(st​,at​)−vπw​(st​), where the Q-function is approximated by the Monte Carlo return ∑k=tTrk\sum_{k=t}^T r_k∑k=tT​rk​. The full gradient estimate for a trajectory is then the sum over all timesteps:

g^=∑t=0TZcv,t=∑t=0T∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st)(Gt−vπw(st))\hat{g} = \sum_{t=0}^T Z_{\text{cv},t} = \sum_{t=0}^T \nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)\left(G_t - v^{\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}}(s_t)\right)g^​=t=0∑T​Zcv,t​=t=0∑T​∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​)(Gt​−vπw​(st​))
(27)

In practice, we do not have access to the true value function and must learn it. Unlike the methods in the amortization chapter, where we learned value functions to approximate the optimal Q-function, here our goal is policy evaluation: estimating the value of the current policy πw\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}πw​. The same function approximation techniques apply, but we target vπwv^{\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}}vπw​ rather than v∗v^*v∗. The simplest approach is to regress from states to Monte Carlo returns, learning what Williams (1992) called a “baseline”:

Algorithm 2 (Policy Gradient with Simple Baseline)

Input: Policy parameterization πw(a∣s)\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a|s)πw​(a∣s), baseline function b(s;θ)b(s;\boldsymbol{\theta})b(s;θ)
Output: Updated policy parameters w\boldsymbol{w}w
Hyperparameters: Learning rates αw\alpha_wαw​, αθ\alpha_\thetaαθ​, number of episodes NNN, episode length TTT

  1. Initialize parameters w\boldsymbol{w}w, θ\boldsymbol{\theta}θ

  2. For episode = 1, ..., NNN do:

    1. Collect trajectory τ=(s0,a0,r0,...,sT,aT,rT)\tau = (s_0, a_0, r_0, ..., s_T, a_T, r_T)τ=(s0​,a0​,r0​,...,sT​,aT​,rT​) using policy πw(a∣s)\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a|s)πw​(a∣s)

    2. Compute returns: Gt=∑k=tTrkG_t = \sum_{k=t}^T r_kGt​=∑k=tT​rk​ for t=0,...,Tt = 0, ..., Tt=0,...,T

    3. Update baseline: θ←θ−αθ∇θ∑t=0T(Gt−b(st;θ))2\boldsymbol{\theta} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\theta} - \alpha_\theta \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\sum_{t=0}^T (G_t - b(s_t;\boldsymbol{\theta}))^2θ←θ−αθ​∇θ​∑t=0T​(Gt​−b(st​;θ))2

    4. Compute gradient estimate: g^=∑t=0T∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st)(Gt−b(st;θ))\hat{g} = \sum_{t=0}^T \nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)(G_t - b(s_t;\boldsymbol{\theta}))g^​=∑t=0T​∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​)(Gt​−b(st​;θ))

    5. Update policy: w←w+αwg^\boldsymbol{w} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{w} + \alpha_w \hat{g}w←w+αw​g^​

  3. Return w\boldsymbol{w}w

When implementing this algorithm nowadays, we always use mini-batching to make full use of our GPUs. Therefore, a more representative variant for this algorithm would be:

Algorithm 3 (Policy Gradient with Optimal Control Variate and Mini-batches)

Input: Policy parameterization πw(a∣s)\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a|s)πw​(a∣s), value function v(s;θ)v(s;\boldsymbol{\theta})v(s;θ)
Output: Updated policy parameters w\boldsymbol{w}w
Hyperparameters: Learning rates αw\alpha_wαw​, αθ\alpha_\thetaαθ​, number of iterations NNN, episode length TTT, batch size BBB, mini-batch size MMM

  1. Initialize parameters w\boldsymbol{w}w, θ\boldsymbol{\theta}θ

  2. For iteration = 1, ..., N:

    1. Initialize empty buffer D\mathcal{D}D

    2. For b = 1, ..., B:

      1. Collect trajectory τb=(s0,a0,r0,...,sT,aT,rT)\tau_b = (s_0, a_0, r_0, ..., s_T, a_T, r_T)τb​=(s0​,a0​,r0​,...,sT​,aT​,rT​) using policy πw(a∣s)\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a|s)πw​(a∣s)

      2. Compute returns: Gt=∑k=tTrkG_t = \sum_{k=t}^T r_kGt​=∑k=tT​rk​ for all t

      3. Store tuple (st,at,Gt)t=0T(s_t, a_t, G_t)_{t=0}^T(st​,at​,Gt​)t=0T​ in D\mathcal{D}D

    3. For value_epoch = 1, ..., K:

      1. Sample mini-batch Bv\mathcal{B}_vBv​ of size MMM from D\mathcal{D}D

      2. Compute value loss: Lv=1M∑(s,a,G)∈Bv(v(s;θ)−G)2L_v = \frac{1}{M}\sum_{(s,a,G) \in \mathcal{B}_v} (v(s;\boldsymbol{\theta}) - G)^2Lv​=M1​∑(s,a,G)∈Bv​​(v(s;θ)−G)2

      3. Update value function: θ←θ−αθ∇θLv\boldsymbol{\theta} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\theta} - \alpha_\theta \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}L_vθ←θ−αθ​∇θ​Lv​

    4. Compute advantages: A(s,a)=G−v(s;θ)A(s,a) = G - v(s;\boldsymbol{\theta})A(s,a)=G−v(s;θ) for all (s,a,G)∈D(s,a,G) \in \mathcal{D}(s,a,G)∈D

    5. Normalize advantages: A←A−μAσAA \leftarrow \frac{A - \mu_A}{\sigma_A}A←σA​A−μA​​

    6. For policy_epoch = 1, ..., J:

      1. Sample mini-batch Bπ\mathcal{B}_\piBπ​ of size MMM from D\mathcal{D}D

      2. Compute policy loss: Lπ=−1M∑(s,a,A)∈Bπlog⁡πw(a∣s)AL_\pi = -\frac{1}{M}\sum_{(s,a,A) \in \mathcal{B}_\pi} \log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a|s)ALπ​=−M1​∑(s,a,A)∈Bπ​​logπw​(a∣s)A

      3. Update policy: w←w−αw∇wLπ\boldsymbol{w} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{w} - \alpha_w \nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}L_\piw←w−αw​∇w​Lπ​

  3. Return w\boldsymbol{w}w

The value function is trained by regressing states directly to their sampled Monte Carlo returns GGG. Advantage normalization (step 2.5) is not part of the optimal baseline derivation but improves optimization in practice and is standard in modern implementations.

Generalized Advantage Estimation¶

The baseline construction gave us a gradient estimator of the form:

∇wJ(w)≈1N∑i=1N∑t=0T∇wlog⁡πw(at(i)∣st(i))(Gt(i)−v(st(i)))\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}J(\boldsymbol{w}) \approx \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{t=0}^T \nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t^{(i)}|s_t^{(i)}) \left(G_t^{(i)} - v(s_t^{(i)})\right)∇w​J(w)≈N1​i=1∑N​t=0∑T​∇w​logπw​(at(i)​∣st(i)​)(Gt(i)​−v(st(i)​))
(28)

where Gt=∑k=tTrkG_t = \sum_{k=t}^T r_kGt​=∑k=tT​rk​ is the Monte Carlo return from time ttt. For each visited state-action pair (st,at)(s_t, a_t)(st​,at​), the term in parentheses

A^tMC=Gt−v(st)\widehat{A}_t^{\text{MC}} = G_t - v(s_t)AtMC​=Gt​−v(st​)
(29)

is a Monte Carlo estimate of the advantage Aπ(st,at)=qπ(st,at)−vπ(st)A^{\pi}(s_t, a_t) = q^{\pi}(s_t, a_t) - v^{\pi}(s_t)Aπ(st​,at​)=qπ(st​,at​)−vπ(st​). If the baseline equals the true value function, v=vπv = v^{\pi}v=vπ, then E[A^tMC∣st,at]=Aπ(st,at)\mathbb{E}[\widehat{A}_t^{\text{MC}} | s_t, a_t] = A^{\pi}(s_t, a_t)E[AtMC​∣st​,at​]=Aπ(st​,at​), so this estimator is unbiased.

However, as an estimator it has two limitations. First, it has high variance because GtG_tGt​ depends on all future rewards. Second, it uses the value function only as a baseline, not as a predictor of long-term returns. We essentially discard the information in v(st+1),v(st+2),…v(s_{t+1}), v(s_{t+2}), \ldotsv(st+1​),v(st+2​),…

GAE addresses these issues by constructing a family of estimators that interpolate between pure Monte Carlo and pure bootstrapping. A parameter λ\lambdaλ controls the bias-variance tradeoff.

Decomposing the Monte Carlo Advantage¶

Fix a value function v(s)v(s)v(s) (not necessarily equal to vπv^{\pi}vπ) and define the one-step residual:

δt=rt+γv(st+1)−v(st)\delta_t = r_t + \gamma v(s_{t+1}) - v(s_t)δt​=rt​+γv(st+1​)−v(st​)
(30)

Start from the Monte Carlo advantage and add and subtract γv(st+1)\gamma v(s_{t+1})γv(st+1​):

Gt−v(st)=rt+γGt+1−v(st)=rt+γv(st+1)−v(st)+γ(Gt+1−v(st+1))=δt+γ(Gt+1−v(st+1))\begin{align*} G_t - v(s_t) &= r_t + \gamma G_{t+1} - v(s_t) \\ &= r_t + \gamma v(s_{t+1}) - v(s_t) + \gamma(G_{t+1} - v(s_{t+1})) \\ &= \delta_t + \gamma(G_{t+1} - v(s_{t+1})) \end{align*}Gt​−v(st​)​=rt​+γGt+1​−v(st​)=rt​+γv(st+1​)−v(st​)+γ(Gt+1​−v(st+1​))=δt​+γ(Gt+1​−v(st+1​))​
(31)

Applying this decomposition recursively yields:

Gt−v(st)=∑l=0T−tγlδt+lG_t - v(s_t) = \sum_{l=0}^{T-t} \gamma^l \delta_{t+l}Gt​−v(st​)=l=0∑T−t​γlδt+l​
(32)

The Monte Carlo advantage is exactly the discounted sum of future residuals. This is an algebraic identity, not an approximation.

The sequence {δt+l}l≥0\{\delta_{t+l}\}_{l \geq 0}{δt+l​}l≥0​ provides incremental corrections to the value function as we move forward in time. The term δt\delta_tδt​ depends only on (st,at,st+1)(s_t, a_t, s_{t+1})(st​,at​,st+1​); δt+1\delta_{t+1}δt+1​ depends on (st+1,at+1,st+2)(s_{t+1}, a_{t+1}, s_{t+2})(st+1​,at+1​,st+2​), and so on. As lll increases, the corrections become more noisy (they depend on more random outcomes) and more sensitive to errors in the value function at later states. Although the full sum is unbiased when v=vπv = v^{\pi}v=vπ, it can have high variance and can be badly affected by approximation error in vvv.

GAE as a Shrinkage Estimator¶

The decomposition above suggests a family of estimators that downweight residuals farther in the future. Let λ∈[0,1]\lambda \in [0,1]λ∈[0,1] and define:

Atλ=∑l=0T−t(γλ)lδt+lA_t^{\lambda} = \sum_{l=0}^{T-t} (\gamma\lambda)^l \delta_{t+l}Atλ​=l=0∑T−t​(γλ)lδt+l​
(33)

This is the generalized advantage estimator AtGAE(γ,λ)A_t^{\text{GAE}(\gamma,\lambda)}AtGAE(γ,λ)​.

Two special cases illustrate the extremes. When λ=1\lambda = 1λ=1, we recover the Monte Carlo advantage:

Atλ=1=∑l=0T−tγlδt+l=Gt−v(st)A_t^{\lambda=1} = \sum_{l=0}^{T-t} \gamma^l \delta_{t+l} = G_t - v(s_t)Atλ=1​=l=0∑T−t​γlδt+l​=Gt​−v(st​)
(34)

When λ=0\lambda = 0λ=0, we keep only the immediate residual:

Atλ=0=δt=rt+γv(st+1)−v(st)A_t^{\lambda=0} = \delta_t = r_t + \gamma v(s_{t+1}) - v(s_t)Atλ=0​=δt​=rt​+γv(st+1​)−v(st​)
(35)

Intermediate values 0<λ<10 < \lambda < 10<λ<1 interpolate between these extremes. The influence of δt+l\delta_{t+l}δt+l​ decays geometrically as (γλ)l(\gamma\lambda)^l(γλ)l. The parameter λ\lambdaλ acts as a shrinkage parameter: small λ\lambdaλ shrinks the estimator toward the one-step residual; large λ\lambdaλ allows the estimator to behave more like the Monte Carlo advantage.

If v=vπv = v^{\pi}v=vπ is the true value function, then E[δt∣st,at]=Aπ(st,at)\mathbb{E}[\delta_t | s_t, a_t] = A^{\pi}(s_t, a_t)E[δt​∣st​,at​]=Aπ(st​,at​) and E[δt+l∣st,at]=0\mathbb{E}[\delta_{t+l} | s_t, a_t] = 0E[δt+l​∣st​,at​]=0 for l≥1l \geq 1l≥1. In this case:

E[Atλ∣st,at]=∑l=0T−t(γλ)lE[δt+l∣st,at]=Aπ(st,at)\mathbb{E}[A_t^{\lambda} | s_t, a_t] = \sum_{l=0}^{T-t} (\gamma\lambda)^l \mathbb{E}[\delta_{t+l} | s_t, a_t] = A^{\pi}(s_t, a_t)E[Atλ​∣st​,at​]=l=0∑T−t​(γλ)lE[δt+l​∣st​,at​]=Aπ(st​,at​)
(36)

for all λ∈[0,1]\lambda \in [0,1]λ∈[0,1]. When the value function is exact, GAE is unbiased regardless of λ\lambdaλ; changing λ\lambdaλ only affects variance.

In practice, we approximate vπv^{\pi}vπ with a function approximator, and the residuals δt+l\delta_{t+l}δt+l​ inherit approximation error. Distant residuals involve multiple applications of the approximate value function and are more contaminated by modeling error. Downweighting them (choosing λ<1\lambda < 1λ<1) introduces bias but can reduce variance and limit the impact of those errors.

Mixture of Multi-Step Estimators¶

Another perspective on GAE comes from multi-step returns. Define the kkk-step return from time ttt:

Gt(k)=∑l=0k−1γlrt+l+γkv(st+k)G_t^{(k)} = \sum_{l=0}^{k-1} \gamma^l r_{t+l} + \gamma^k v(s_{t+k})Gt(k)​=l=0∑k−1​γlrt+l​+γkv(st+k​)
(37)

and the corresponding kkk-step advantage estimator At(k)=Gt(k)−v(st)A_t^{(k)} = G_t^{(k)} - v(s_t)At(k)​=Gt(k)​−v(st​). Each At(k)A_t^{(k)}At(k)​ uses kkk rewards before bootstrapping; larger kkk means more variance but less bootstrapping error.

The GAE estimator can be written as a geometric mixture:

Atλ=(1−λ)∑k=1T−tλk−1At(k)A_t^{\lambda} = (1-\lambda) \sum_{k=1}^{T-t} \lambda^{k-1} A_t^{(k)}Atλ​=(1−λ)k=1∑T−t​λk−1At(k)​
(38)

GAE is a weighted average of the kkk-step advantage estimators, with shorter horizons weighted more heavily when λ\lambdaλ is small.

Using GAE in the Policy Gradient¶

Once we choose λ\lambdaλ, we plug AtλA_t^{\lambda}Atλ​ in place of Gt−v(st)G_t - v(s_t)Gt​−v(st​) in the policy gradient estimator:

∇wJ(w)≈1N∑i=1N∑t=0T∇wlog⁡πw(at(i)∣st(i))Atλ,(i)\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}J(\boldsymbol{w}) \approx \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{t=0}^T \nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t^{(i)}|s_t^{(i)}) A_t^{\lambda,(i)}∇w​J(w)≈N1​i=1∑N​t=0∑T​∇w​logπw​(at(i)​∣st(i)​)Atλ,(i)​
(39)

We still use a control variate to reduce variance (the baseline vvv), but now we construct the advantage target by smoothing the sequence of residuals {δt}\{\delta_t\}{δt​} with a geometrically decaying kernel.

For the value function, it is convenient to define the λ\lambdaλ-return:

Gtλ=Atλ+v(st)G_t^{\lambda} = A_t^{\lambda} + v(s_t)Gtλ​=Atλ​+v(st​)
(40)

When λ=1\lambda = 1λ=1, GtλG_t^{\lambda}Gtλ​ reduces to the Monte Carlo return; when λ=0\lambda = 0λ=0, it becomes the one-step bootstrapped target rt+γv(st+1)r_t + \gamma v(s_{t+1})rt​+γv(st+1​).

Algorithm 4 (Policy Gradient with GAE and Mini-batches)

Input: Policy parameterization πw(a∣s)\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a|s)πw​(a∣s), value function v(s;θ)v(s;\boldsymbol{\theta})v(s;θ)
Output: Updated policy parameters w\boldsymbol{w}w
Hyperparameters: Learning rates αw\alpha_wαw​, αθ\alpha_\thetaαθ​, number of iterations NNN, episode length TTT, batch size BBB, mini-batch size MMM, discount γ\gammaγ, GAE parameter λ\lambdaλ

  1. Initialize parameters w\boldsymbol{w}w, θ\boldsymbol{\theta}θ

  2. For iteration = 1, ..., NNN:

    1. Initialize empty buffer D\mathcal{D}D

    2. For b=1,...,Bb = 1, ..., Bb=1,...,B:

      1. Collect trajectory τb=(s0,a0,r0,...,sT,aT,rT)\tau_b = (s_0, a_0, r_0, ..., s_T, a_T, r_T)τb​=(s0​,a0​,r0​,...,sT​,aT​,rT​) using policy πw(a∣s)\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a|s)πw​(a∣s)

      2. Compute value predictions vt=v(st;θ)v_t = v(s_t;\boldsymbol{\theta})vt​=v(st​;θ) for t=0,…,Tt = 0, \ldots, Tt=0,…,T and set vT+1=0v_{T+1} = 0vT+1​=0

      3. Compute residuals: δt=rt+γvt+1−vt\delta_t = r_t + \gamma v_{t+1} - v_tδt​=rt​+γvt+1​−vt​ for t=0,…,Tt = 0, \ldots, Tt=0,…,T

      4. Compute GAE advantages backwards:

        1. Set AT=δTA_T = \delta_TAT​=δT​

        2. For t=T−1,...,0t = T-1, ..., 0t=T−1,...,0: At=δt+(γλ)At+1A_t = \delta_t + (\gamma\lambda) A_{t+1}At​=δt​+(γλ)At+1​

      5. Compute λ\lambdaλ-returns: Gtλ=At+vtG_t^{\lambda} = A_t + v_tGtλ​=At​+vt​ for t=0,…,Tt = 0, \ldots, Tt=0,…,T

      6. Store tuples (st,at,At,Gtλ)t=0T(s_t, a_t, A_t, G_t^{\lambda})_{t=0}^T(st​,at​,At​,Gtλ​)t=0T​ in D\mathcal{D}D

    3. For value_epoch = 1, ..., KKK:

      1. Sample mini-batch Bv\mathcal{B}_vBv​ of size MMM from D\mathcal{D}D

      2. Compute value loss: Lv=1M∑(s,⋅,⋅,Gλ)∈Bv(v(s;θ)−Gλ)2L_v = \frac{1}{M}\sum_{(s,\cdot,\cdot,G^{\lambda}) \in \mathcal{B}_v} (v(s;\boldsymbol{\theta}) - G^{\lambda})^2Lv​=M1​∑(s,⋅,⋅,Gλ)∈Bv​​(v(s;θ)−Gλ)2

      3. Update value function: θ←θ−αθ∇θLv\boldsymbol{\theta} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\theta} - \alpha_\theta \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}L_vθ←θ−αθ​∇θ​Lv​

    4. Normalize advantages: A←A−μAσAA \leftarrow \frac{A - \mu_A}{\sigma_A}A←σA​A−μA​​

    5. For policy_epoch = 1, ..., JJJ:

      1. Sample mini-batch Bπ\mathcal{B}_\piBπ​ of size MMM from D\mathcal{D}D

      2. Compute policy loss: Lπ=−1M∑(s,a,A,⋅)∈Bπlog⁡πw(a∣s)AL_\pi = -\frac{1}{M}\sum_{(s,a,A,\cdot) \in \mathcal{B}_\pi} \log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a|s) ALπ​=−M1​∑(s,a,A,⋅)∈Bπ​​logπw​(a∣s)A

      3. Update policy: w←w−αw∇wLπ\boldsymbol{w} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{w} - \alpha_w \nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}L_\piw←w−αw​∇w​Lπ​

  3. Return w\boldsymbol{w}w

When λ=1\lambda = 1λ=1, this reduces (up to advantage normalization) to the Monte Carlo baseline algorithm earlier in the chapter. When λ=0\lambda = 0λ=0, advantages become the one-step residuals δt\delta_tδt​, and the λ\lambdaλ-returns reduce to standard one-step bootstrapped targets.

Actor-Critic as the λ=0\lambda = 0λ=0 Limit¶

The case λ=0\lambda = 0λ=0 is particularly simple. The advantage becomes:

Atλ=0=δt=rt+γv(st+1)−v(st)A_t^{\lambda=0} = \delta_t = r_t + \gamma v(s_{t+1}) - v(s_t)Atλ=0​=δt​=rt​+γv(st+1​)−v(st​)
(41)

and the policy update reduces to:

w←w+αw∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st)δt\boldsymbol{w} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{w} + \alpha_w \nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t) \delta_tw←w+αw​∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​)δt​
(42)

while the value update becomes a standard one-step regression toward rt+γv(st+1)r_t + \gamma v(s_{t+1})rt​+γv(st+1​). This gives the online actor-critic algorithm:

Algorithm 5 (Actor-Critic with One-Step Residuals)

Input: Policy parameterization πw(a∣s)\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a|s)πw​(a∣s), value function v(s;θ)v(s;\boldsymbol{\theta})v(s;θ)
Output: Updated policy parameters w\boldsymbol{w}w
Hyperparameters: Learning rates αw\alpha_wαw​, αθ\alpha_\thetaαθ​, number of episodes NNN, episode length TTT, discount γ\gammaγ

  1. Initialize parameters w\boldsymbol{w}w, θ\boldsymbol{\theta}θ

  2. For episode = 1, ..., NNN do:

    1. Initialize state s0s_0s0​

    2. For t=0,...,Tt = 0, ..., Tt=0,...,T do:

      1. Sample action: at∼πw(⋅∣st)a_t \sim \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(\cdot|s_t)at​∼πw​(⋅∣st​)

      2. Execute ata_tat​, observe rtr_trt​, st+1s_{t+1}st+1​

      3. Compute residual: δt=rt+γv(st+1;θ)−v(st;θ)\delta_t = r_t + \gamma v(s_{t+1};\boldsymbol{\theta}) - v(s_t;\boldsymbol{\theta})δt​=rt​+γv(st+1​;θ)−v(st​;θ)

      4. Update value function: θ←θ+αθδt∇θv(st;θ)\boldsymbol{\theta} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\theta} + \alpha_\theta \delta_t \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}v(s_t;\boldsymbol{\theta})θ←θ+αθ​δt​∇θ​v(st​;θ)

      5. Update policy: w←w+αw∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st)δt\boldsymbol{w} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{w} + \alpha_w \nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t) \delta_tw←w+αw​∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​)δt​

  3. Return w\boldsymbol{w}w

This algorithm was derived by Sutton in his 1984 thesis as an “adaptive heuristic” for temporal credit assignment. In the language of this chapter, it is the λ=0\lambda = 0λ=0 member of the GAE family: it uses the most local residual δt\delta_tδt​ as both the target for the value function and the advantage estimate for the policy gradient.

Likelihood Ratio Methods in Reinforcement Learning¶

How do importance ratios and constrained or clipped surrogates reuse trajectories collected under an earlier policy?

The score function estimator from the previous section is a special case of the likelihood ratio method where the proposal distribution equals the target distribution. We now consider the general case where they differ.

Recall the likelihood ratio gradient estimator from the beginning of this chapter. For objective J(θ)=Ex∼p(x;θ)[f(x)]J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x;\theta)}[f(x)]J(θ)=Ex∼p(x;θ)​[f(x)] and any proposal distribution q(x)q(x)q(x):

∇θJ(θ)=Ex∼q(x)[f(x)ρ(x;q,θ)∇θlog⁡p(x;θ)]\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim q(x)}\left[f(x) \rho(x; q, \theta) \nabla_\theta \log p(x;\theta)\right]∇θ​J(θ)=Ex∼q(x)​[f(x)ρ(x;q,θ)∇θ​logp(x;θ)]
(43)

where ρ(x;q,θ)=p(x;θ)q(x)\rho(x; q, \theta) = \frac{p(x;\theta)}{q(x)}ρ(x;q,θ)=q(x)p(x;θ)​ is the likelihood ratio. The partial derivative ∂ρ∂θ=ρ∇θlog⁡p\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial \theta} = \rho \nabla_\theta \log p∂θ∂ρ​=ρ∇θ​logp holds because xxx is treated as fixed, having been sampled from qqq, which does not depend on θ\thetaθ.

In reinforcement learning, let x=τx = \taux=τ be a trajectory, f(τ)=G(τ)f(\tau) = G(\tau)f(τ)=G(τ) the return, p(τ;w)p(\tau;\boldsymbol{w})p(τ;w) the trajectory distribution under policy πw\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}πw​, and q(τ)q(\tau)q(τ) the trajectory distribution under some other policy πq\pi_qπq​. The gradient becomes:

∇wJ(w)=Eτ∼πq[G(τ)ρ(τ)∑t=0T∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st)]\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}} J(\boldsymbol{w}) = \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim \pi_q}\left[G(\tau) \rho(\tau) \sum_{t=0}^T \nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}} \log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)\right]∇w​J(w)=Eτ∼πq​​[G(τ)ρ(τ)t=0∑T​∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​)]
(44)

where the trajectory likelihood ratio simplifies because transition probabilities cancel:

ρ(τ)=p(τ;w)q(τ)=∏t=0Tπw(at∣st)πq(at∣st)=∏t=0Tρt\rho(\tau) = \frac{p(\tau;\boldsymbol{w})}{q(\tau)} = \prod_{t=0}^T \frac{\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)}{\pi_q(a_t|s_t)} = \prod_{t=0}^T \rho_tρ(τ)=q(τ)p(τ;w)​=t=0∏T​πq​(at​∣st​)πw​(at​∣st​)​=t=0∏T​ρt​
(45)

This product of T+1T+1T+1 ratios can become extremely large or small as TTT grows, leading to high variance. The temporal structure provides some relief: since Ea∼πq[ρ]=1\mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi_q}[\rho] = 1Ea∼πq​​[ρ]=1, future ratios ρk\rho_{k}ρk​ for k>tk > tk>t that do not affect the reward rtr_trt​ can be marginalized out. However, past ratios ρ0:t−1\rho_{0:t-1}ρ0:t−1​ are still needed to correctly weight the probability of reaching state sts_tst​.

In practice, algorithms like PPO and TRPO make an additional approximation: they use only the per-step ratio ρt\rho_tρt​ rather than the cumulative product ρ0:t\rho_{0:t}ρ0:t​. This ignores the mismatch between the state distributions induced by the two policies. Combined with a baseline b(st)b(s_t)b(st​), the approximate estimator is:

∇wJ(w)≈Eτ∼πq[∑t=0Tρt∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st)(Gt−b(st))]\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}} J(\boldsymbol{w}) \approx \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim \pi_q}\left[\sum_{t=0}^T \rho_t \nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}} \log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t) (G_t - b(s_t))\right]∇w​J(w)≈Eτ∼πq​​[t=0∑T​ρt​∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​)(Gt​−b(st​))]
(46)

(47)

where At=Gt−b(st)A_t = G_t - b(s_t)At​=Gt​−b(st​). Taking the gradient with respect to w\boldsymbol{w}w, only ρt\rho_tρt​ depends on w\boldsymbol{w}w (since trajectories are sampled from πq\pi_qπq​):

∇wLIS(w)=Eτ∼πq[∑t=0TAt∇wρt]\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}} L^{\text{IS}}(\boldsymbol{w}) = \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim \pi_q}\left[\sum_{t=0}^T A_t \nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}} \rho_t\right]∇w​LIS(w)=Eτ∼πq​​[t=0∑T​At​∇w​ρt​]
(48)

∇wρt=∇wπw(at∣st)πq(at∣st)=∇wπw(at∣st)πq(at∣st)=ρt∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st)\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}} \rho_t = \nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}} \frac{\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)}{\pi_q(a_t|s_t)} = \frac{\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}} \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)}{\pi_q(a_t|s_t)} = \rho_t \nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}} \log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)∇w​ρt​=∇w​πq​(at​∣st​)πw​(at​∣st​)​=πq​(at​∣st​)∇w​πw​(at​∣st​)​=ρt​∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​)
(49)

Substituting back:

∇wLIS(w)=Eτ∼πq[∑t=0Tρt∇wlog⁡πw(at∣st)At]\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}} L^{\text{IS}}(\boldsymbol{w}) = \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim \pi_q}\left[\sum_{t=0}^T \rho_t \nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}} \log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t) A_t\right]∇w​LIS(w)=Eτ∼πq​​[t=0∑T​ρt​∇w​logπw​(at​∣st​)At​]
(50)

This matches equation (46). When πq=πw\pi_q = \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}πq​=πw​, the ratios ρt=1\rho_t = 1ρt​=1 and we recover the score function estimator. The approximation error grows as the policies diverge, which motivates the trust region and clipping mechanisms discussed below.

Variance and the Dominance Condition¶

The ratio ρt=πw(at∣st)/πq(at∣st)\rho_t = \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)/\pi_q(a_t|s_t)ρt​=πw​(at​∣st​)/πq​(at​∣st​) is well-behaved only when the two policies are similar. If πw\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}πw​ assigns high probability to an action where πq\pi_qπq​ assigns low probability, the ratio explodes. For example, if πq(a∣s)=0.01\pi_q(a|s) = 0.01πq​(a∣s)=0.01 and πw(a∣s)=0.5\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a|s) = 0.5πw​(a∣s)=0.5, then ρ=50\rho = 50ρ=50, amplifying any noise in the advantage estimate.

Importance sampling also requires the dominance condition: the support of πw\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}πw​ must be contained in the support of πq\pi_qπq​. If πw(a∣s)>0\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a|s) > 0πw​(a∣s)>0 but πq(a∣s)=0\pi_q(a|s) = 0πq​(a∣s)=0, the ratio is undefined. Stochastic policies typically have full support, but the ratio can still become arbitrarily large as πq(a∣s)→0\pi_q(a|s) \to 0πq​(a∣s)→0.

A common use case is to set πq=πwold\pi_q = \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}_{\text{old}}}πq​=πwold​​, a previous version of the policy. This allows reusing data across multiple gradient steps: collect trajectories once, then update w\boldsymbol{w}w several times. But each update moves w\boldsymbol{w}w further from wold\boldsymbol{w}_{\text{old}}wold​, making the ratios more extreme. Eventually, the gradient signal is dominated by a few samples with large weights.

Proximal Policy Optimization¶

The variance issues suggest a natural solution: keep the ratio ρt\rho_tρt​ close to 1 by ensuring the new policy stays close to the behavior policy. This keeps the importance-weighted surrogate LIS(w)L^{\text{IS}}(\boldsymbol{w})LIS(w) from (47) well-behaved.

Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO) formalizes this by adding a constraint on the KL divergence between the old and new policies:

max⁡wLIS(w)subject toEs[DKL(πwold(⋅∣s)∥πw(⋅∣s))]≤δ\max_{\boldsymbol{w}} L^{\text{IS}}(\boldsymbol{w}) \quad \text{subject to} \quad \mathbb{E}_s\left[D_{\text{KL}}(\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}_{\text{old}}}(\cdot|s) \| \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(\cdot|s))\right] \leq \deltawmax​LIS(w)subject toEs​[DKL​(πwold​​(⋅∣s)∥πw​(⋅∣s))]≤δ
(51)

The KL constraint ensures that the two distributions remain similar, which bounds how extreme the importance weights can become. This is a constrained optimization problem, and one could in principle apply standard methods such as projected gradient descent or augmented Lagrangian approaches (as discussed in the trajectory optimization chapter). TRPO takes a different approach: it uses a second-order Taylor approximation of the KL constraint around the current parameters and solves the resulting trust region subproblem using conjugate gradient methods. This involves computing the Fisher information matrix (the Hessian of the KL divergence), which adds computational overhead.

Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) achieves similar behavior through a simpler mechanism: rather than constraining the distributions to be similar, it directly clips the ratio ρt\rho_tρt​ to prevent it from moving too far from 1. This is a construction-level guarantee rather than an optimization-level constraint.

From Trajectory Expectations to State-Action Averages¶

Before defining the PPO objective, we need to clarify the relationship between the trajectory-level surrogate (47) and the state-action level objective that PPO actually optimizes. The importance-weighted surrogate is defined as an expectation over trajectories:

LIS(w)=Eτ∼πq[∑t=0TρtAt]L^{\text{IS}}(\boldsymbol{w}) = \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim \pi_q}\left[\sum_{t=0}^T \rho_t A_t\right]LIS(w)=Eτ∼πq​​[t=0∑T​ρt​At​]
(52)

We can rewrite this as an expectation over state-action pairs by introducing a sampling distribution. For a finite horizon TTT, define the averaged time-marginal distribution:

ξπq(s,a)=1T+1∑t=0Tdtπq(s)πq(a∣s)\xi_{\pi_q}(s, a) = \frac{1}{T+1} \sum_{t=0}^{T} d_t^{\pi_q}(s) \pi_q(a|s)ξπq​​(s,a)=T+11​t=0∑T​dtπq​​(s)πq​(a∣s)
(53)

where dtπq(s)d_t^{\pi_q}(s)dtπq​​(s) is the probability of being in state sss at time ttt when following policy πq\pi_qπq​ from the initial distribution. This is the uniform mixture over the time-indexed state-action distributions: we pick a timestep ttt uniformly at random from {0,1,…,T}\{0, 1, \ldots, T\}{0,1,…,T}, then sample (s,a)(s, a)(s,a) from the joint distribution at that timestep.

With this definition, the trajectory expectation becomes:

Eτ∼πq[∑t=0TρtAt]=(T+1)⋅E(s,a)∼ξπq[ρ(s,a)A(s,a)]\mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim \pi_q}\left[\sum_{t=0}^T \rho_t A_t\right] = (T+1) \cdot \mathbb{E}_{(s,a) \sim \xi_{\pi_q}}\left[\rho(s, a) A(s, a)\right]Eτ∼πq​​[t=0∑T​ρt​At​]=(T+1)⋅E(s,a)∼ξπq​​​[ρ(s,a)A(s,a)]
(54)

The factor (T+1)(T+1)(T+1) is just a constant that does not affect the optimization. This reformulation shows that the importance-weighted surrogate is equivalent to an expectation over state-action pairs drawn from the averaged time-marginal distribution. This is not a stationary distribution or a discounted visitation distribution, but the empirical mixture induced by the finite-horizon rollout procedure.

The Clipped Surrogate Objective¶

PPO replaces the linear importance-weighted term ρA\rho AρA with a clipped version. For a state-action pair (s,a)(s, a)(s,a) with advantage AAA and importance ratio ρ(w)=πw(a∣s)/πwold(a∣s)\rho(\boldsymbol{w}) = \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a|s) / \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}_{\text{old}}}(a|s)ρ(w)=πw​(a∣s)/πwold​​(a∣s), define the per-sample clipped objective:

ℓCLIP(w;s,a,A)=min⁡(ρ(w)A, clip(ρ(w),1−ϵ,1+ϵ)A)\ell^{\text{CLIP}}(\boldsymbol{w}; s, a, A) = \min\left(\rho(\boldsymbol{w}) A, \, \text{clip}(\rho(\boldsymbol{w}), 1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon) A\right)ℓCLIP(w;s,a,A)=min(ρ(w)A,clip(ρ(w),1−ϵ,1+ϵ)A)
(55)

where ϵ\epsilonϵ is a hyperparameter (typically 0.1 or 0.2) and clip(x,a,b)=max⁡(a,min⁡(x,b))\text{clip}(x, a, b) = \max(a, \min(x, b))clip(x,a,b)=max(a,min(x,b)) restricts xxx to the interval [a,b][a, b][a,b].

The population-level PPO objective is then:

LCLIP(w)=E(s,a,A)∼ξπwold[ℓCLIP(w;s,a,A)]L^{\text{CLIP}}(\boldsymbol{w}) = \mathbb{E}_{(s,a,A) \sim \xi_{\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}_{\text{old}}}}}\left[\ell^{\text{CLIP}}(\boldsymbol{w}; s, a, A)\right]LCLIP(w)=E(s,a,A)∼ξπwold​​​​[ℓCLIP(w;s,a,A)]
(56)

where the expectation is taken over the averaged time-marginal distribution (53) induced by πwold\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}_{\text{old}}}πwold​​.

In practice, we never compute this expectation exactly. Instead, we collect a batch of transitions D={(st(i),at(i),At(i))}\mathcal{D} = \{(s_t^{(i)}, a_t^{(i)}, A_t^{(i)})\}D={(st(i)​,at(i)​,At(i)​)} by running πwold\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}_{\text{old}}}πwold​​ and approximate the expectation with an empirical average:

L^CLIP(w;D)=1∣D∣∑(s,a,A)∈DℓCLIP(w;s,a,A)\hat{L}^{\text{CLIP}}(\boldsymbol{w}; \mathcal{D}) = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|} \sum_{(s,a,A) \in \mathcal{D}} \ell^{\text{CLIP}}(\boldsymbol{w}; s, a, A)L^CLIP(w;D)=∣D∣1​(s,a,A)∈D∑​ℓCLIP(w;s,a,A)
(57)

This is the same plug-in approximation used in fitted Q-iteration: replace the unknown population distribution with the empirical distribution P^D\hat{P}_{\mathcal{D}}P^D​ induced by the collected batch, then compute the sample average. The empirical surrogate L^CLIP\hat{L}^{\text{CLIP}}L^CLIP is simply an expectation under P^D\hat{P}_{\mathcal{D}}P^D​. No assumptions about stationarity or discounted visitation are needed. We just average over the transitions we collected.

Intuition for the Clipping Mechanism¶

The min⁡\minmin operator in (55) selects the more pessimistic estimate. Consider the two cases:

  • Positive advantage (A>0A > 0A>0): The action is better than average, so we want to increase πw(a∣s)\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a|s)πw​(a∣s). The unclipped term ρA\rho AρA increases with ρ\rhoρ. The clipped term stops increasing once ρ>1+ϵ\rho > 1 + \epsilonρ>1+ϵ. Taking the minimum means we get the benefit of increasing ρ\rhoρ only up to 1+ϵ1 + \epsilon1+ϵ.

  • Negative advantage (A<0A < 0A<0): The action is worse than average, so we want to decrease πw(a∣s)\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a|s)πw​(a∣s). The unclipped term ρA\rho AρA becomes less negative (improves) as ρ\rhoρ decreases. The clipped term stops improving once ρ<1−ϵ\rho < 1 - \epsilonρ<1−ϵ. Taking the minimum means we get the benefit of decreasing ρ\rhoρ only down to 1−ϵ1 - \epsilon1−ϵ.

In both cases, the clipping removes the incentive to move the probability ratio beyond the interval [1−ϵ,1+ϵ][1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon][1−ϵ,1+ϵ]. This keeps the new policy close to the old policy without explicitly computing or constraining the KL divergence.

Algorithm 6 (Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO-Clip))

Input: Policy πw(a∣s)\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a|s)πw​(a∣s), value function v(s;θ)v(s;\boldsymbol{\theta})v(s;θ)
Output: Updated parameters w\boldsymbol{w}w
Hyperparameters: Clip parameter ϵ\epsilonϵ, learning rates αw\alpha_wαw​, αθ\alpha_\thetaαθ​, number of iterations NNN, batch size BBB, mini-batch size MMM, epochs per iteration KKK, GAE parameters γ\gammaγ, λ\lambdaλ

  1. Initialize parameters w\boldsymbol{w}w, θ\boldsymbol{\theta}θ

  2. For iteration = 1, ..., NNN:

    1. Collect batch D\mathcal{D}D of BBB trajectories using policy πw\pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}πw​

    2. Compute GAE advantages AtA_tAt​ and λ\lambdaλ-returns GtλG_t^{\lambda}Gtλ​ for all timesteps

    3. Store old log-probabilities: log⁡πold(at∣st)=log⁡πw(at∣st)\log \pi_{\text{old}}(a_t|s_t) = \log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a_t|s_t)logπold​(at​∣st​)=logπw​(at​∣st​) for all (st,at)(s_t, a_t)(st​,at​)

    4. Normalize advantages: A←A−μAσAA \leftarrow \frac{A - \mu_A}{\sigma_A}A←σA​A−μA​​

    5. For epoch = 1, ..., KKK:

      1. Shuffle D\mathcal{D}D and partition into mini-batches of size MMM

      2. For each mini-batch B\mathcal{B}B:

        1. Compute ratios: ρ=exp⁡(log⁡πw(a∣s)−log⁡πold(a∣s))\rho = \exp(\log \pi_{\boldsymbol{w}}(a|s) - \log \pi_{\text{old}}(a|s))ρ=exp(logπw​(a∣s)−logπold​(a∣s)) for all (s,a)∈B(s, a) \in \mathcal{B}(s,a)∈B

        2. Compute per-sample objectives: ℓCLIP=min⁡(ρA,clip(ρ,1−ϵ,1+ϵ)A)\ell^{\text{CLIP}} = \min(\rho A, \text{clip}(\rho, 1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon) A)ℓCLIP=min(ρA,clip(ρ,1−ϵ,1+ϵ)A)

        3. Compute empirical surrogate: L^CLIP=1∣B∣∑(s,a,A)∈BℓCLIP\hat{L}^{\text{CLIP}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}|}\sum_{(s,a,A) \in \mathcal{B}} \ell^{\text{CLIP}}L^CLIP=∣B∣1​∑(s,a,A)∈B​ℓCLIP

        4. Compute value loss: Lv=1∣B∣∑(s,Gλ)∈B(v(s;θ)−Gλ)2L_v = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}|}\sum_{(s,G^{\lambda}) \in \mathcal{B}} (v(s;\boldsymbol{\theta}) - G^{\lambda})^2Lv​=∣B∣1​∑(s,Gλ)∈B​(v(s;θ)−Gλ)2

        5. Update policy: w←w+αw∇wL^CLIP\boldsymbol{w} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{w} + \alpha_w \nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}} \hat{L}^{\text{CLIP}}w←w+αw​∇w​L^CLIP

        6. Update value function: θ←θ−αθ∇θLv\boldsymbol{\theta} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\theta} - \alpha_\theta \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} L_vθ←θ−αθ​∇θ​Lv​

  3. Return w\boldsymbol{w}w

The algorithm collects a batch of trajectories, then performs KKK epochs of mini-batch updates on the same data. The empirical surrogate L^CLIP\hat{L}^{\text{CLIP}}L^CLIP approximates the population objective (56) using samples from the averaged time-marginal distribution. The ratio ρ\rhoρ is computed in log-space for numerical stability. Clipping removes the local incentive to move a sampled probability ratio beyond the chosen interval. It does not guarantee that the sampled updates will find a successful policy, and it says nothing about physical constraints absent from the reward or environment.

Experiment: PPO on the SwingRL Plant¶

The SwingRL model from the modeling chapter provides a matched comparison between supplied structure and sampled policy optimization. Both controllers act on the same articulated standing rider, use the same two bounded commands, receive the same observations, and count one full unwrapped rotation as success. The structured controller receives a phase-locked pumping rule whose phases were selected by a model sweep. PPO receives trajectories and the environment reward.

The experiment asks whether the clipped policy-gradient update discovers a full rotation under one fixed, reproducible protocol. The protocol was chosen before inspecting the five final runs.

rollout batch8 environments ×\times× 256 steps
PPO epochs and minibatch4 epochs, 256 samples
optimizerAdam, learning rate 3×10−43\times10^{-4}3×10−4 with linear decay
discount and GAEγ=0.995\gamma=0.995γ=0.995, λ=0.95\lambda=0.95λ=0.95
clipping and entropy coefficients0.2 and 0.001
seeds0, 1, 2, 3, 4
evaluation100 fixed initial states every 50,000 requested interactions

Each complete rollout batch contains 2,048 transitions, so the last update is recorded at 1,001,472 interactions. A checkpoint is the first complete update at or beyond its nominal 50,000-interaction target. Evaluation angles are uniform between −5∘-5^\circ−5∘ and 5∘5^\circ5∘, angular velocities are uniform between -0.1 and 0.1 rad/s, and the deterministic policy uses the tanh of the Gaussian mean. The environment and the structured baseline use the same 100 states.

The replay is an illustration from one prespecified run, not the evidential comparison. Future observations remain hidden until the movie reaches their checkpoint. The five-seed result below carries the comparison across runs.

Download the recorded seed-0 replay

The final policies settle on low-motion behavior. Across the five showcase rollouts, the largest angle lies between 5.45∘5.45^\circ5.45∘ and 5.62∘5.62^\circ5.62∘. Return improves because the policy changes the rider while keeping effort and time penalties modest, but the behavior never approaches the 360∘360^\circ360∘ success condition.

controllertraining transitionsheld-out successmean returnworst suspension tension
structured phase controller0100%191.79-637 N
PPO, mean over five final policies1,001,472 per seed0%-5.11+387 N

The comparison does not establish a general ranking between control and RL. The structured controller receives the oscillation phase and a controller family adapted to the mechanism, while PPO must infer useful coordination from sampled returns. Conversely, the structured controller’s nominal success requires negative suspension tension during 7.37 percent of its active steps. A rigid rod can supply that outward force; a playground chain cannot. PPO avoids the violation by barely moving, which is feasible but does not solve the task.

The two failures answer different audit questions. Optimization has not found a successful sampled policy under this protocol. The successful structured policy exposes an inadequate rigid-link model. More interactions or a revised learning objective might address the first failure. A unilateral chain model or an explicit tension constraint is required for the second.

Suppose the success bonus were increased until PPO learned to rotate the rigid link. Which reported metric would still prevent the result from establishing a successful playground-swing controller? Identify the missing physical mode and describe an evaluation that would expose it.
